trajectory_summary: This is a short, largely one-sided call where a customer who denies making the original inquiry states upfront that he cannot afford solar and has poor credit, and repeats this three times with increasing frustration before the rep asks the direct qualifying question. The rep's 'Gotcha, gotcha' acknowledgments never engage the customer's stated objections, and the call ends in a clean, correct disqualification once credit is confirmed below threshold. There was no viable path to a booked appointment here — the outcome is a legitimate hard DQ, not a lost opportunity — but the rep's handling of the lead-up (three unaddressed statements, an unresolved 'it's not free' legitimacy challenge, and a request to be left alone) reflects reactive listening rather than a controlled qualification flow.
outcome_dispute: v1 tag is unknown/unclear; the observed outcome should be recorded as dq (hard disqualifier: customer confirms credit below the qualifying threshold at 01:44), not a missed-opportunity or no-appointment call. The DQ itself was procedurally correct per qualifiers.credit_qualifier.

primary_coaching_focus.topic: acknowledging stated objections before repeating script
primary_coaching_focus.quote: My credit, I don't have no good credit to get financed solar. You gotta leave me alone.
primary_coaching_focus.why: The customer states his disqualifying credit situation and a request to disengage three times before the rep asks the direct qualifying question at 01:38 — the rep's repeated 'Gotcha, gotcha' response pattern shows he is not actually processing what the customer is saying, just holding space until he can ask his next scripted line.

key_moments.quote: I'm reaching out really quick because we got a request you were looking into solar for your home here in Beaverton.
key_moments.stewart_read: The customer immediately disputes making any request. The rep never grounds the lead source with specificity (form name, date, referral channel) which is exactly the protocol move that reduces suspicion per protocols.how_did_you_get_my_number — instead the vague 'we got a request' framing invites exactly the pushback that follows.

key_moments.stewart_read: This is a legitimacy/scam-anxiety challenge layered on top of a cost objection — the customer is questioning whether 'free' framing is a scam tactic. The rep's response at 01:02 explains installation-fee mechanics but never directly addresses the trust/scam undertone in 'it's not free... you're calling somebody.'

key_moments.quote: My credit, I don't have no good credit to get financed solar. You gotta leave me alone.
key_moments.stewart_read: The customer explicitly states a disqualifying financial fact and asks to be left alone in the same breath. The rep's next line is 'Gotcha. Gotcha. So,' which neither acknowledges the request nor moves to close the call respectfully.

key_moments.quote: This one, I don't have it. No.
key_moments.stewart_read: This is the customer's own disqualifying answer, and ending the call here is correct procedure under the schema's current hard_dq=true rule for stated credit. However, per qualifiers.credit_qualifier's spencer_operator_note, self-reported credit is unreliable (bureau scores often run 30-50 points higher than what customers believe), so a policy question remains open: is DQ-on-stated-credit costing Ion real deals on this floor.
